docs.t: Fed. Cir. — Briefs: 14,000 words; replies 7,000
docs.x: Fed. Cir.. Briefs: 14,000 words; replies 7,000. A principal brief may exceed 30 pages if it has no more than 14,000 words (or 1,300 lines of monospaced text), and a reply may exceed 15 pages if it has no more than 7,000 words (650 lines). In cross-appeals the appellant’s principal brief and its response and reply brief may each run 14,000 words, the appellee’s principal and response brief 16,500, and the appellee’s reply 7,000. Excluded from the count: the certificate of interest, statement of related cases, any addendum, the cover and the exemplary patent claims inside it, and Rule 25.1(e) material, plus the FRAP 32(f) items. A brief over the page limit needs a certificate of compliance, Form 19. (Fed. Cir. R. 32(b), 28.1)

docs.t: Fed. Cir. — 14-point type
docs.x: Fed. Cir.. 14-point type. FRAP 32(a)(5) requires a proportionally spaced serif face of 14 points or larger. That includes footnotes. (FRAP 32(a)(5))

docs.t: Fed. Cir. — Certify compliance
docs.x: Fed. Cir.. Certify compliance. Every brief needs a certificate stating the word count and confirming the typeface and type-style rules are met. (FRAP 32(g))

docs.t: Fed. Cir. — Briefing runs 60 days, then 40, then 21
docs.x: Fed. Cir.. Briefing runs 60 days, then 40, then 21. The appellant’s principal brief is due 60 days after docketing (or 60 days after the certified list or index is served in an agency appeal). The appellee’s or cross-appellant’s principal brief is due 40 days after the appellant’s brief is served. In a cross-appeal the appellant’s response and reply brief is due 40 days after the cross-appellant’s principal and response brief, and the cross-appellant’s reply 21 days after that. A brief answering multiple parties runs from the last one served. A motion that would end the appeal suspends briefing, and if denied the next brief is due in the balance of the time, but not fewer than 14 days from the order. (Fed. Cir. R. 31(a))

docs.t: Fed. Cir. — Certificate of Interest: with your first entry of appearance
docs.x: Fed. Cir.. Certificate of Interest: with your first entry of appearance. Each party, intervenor, amicus, or movant files a certificate of interest at the same time as its first entry of appearance, with negative answers where applicable. It lists every entity represented, any real party in interest, parent corporations and publicly held 10% owners, the law firms and lawyers who appeared below or are expected here but haven’t entered an appearance, and whether related or prior cases exist. It is repeated in each motion, petition, response, principal brief, and amicus brief. The United States and unrepresented individuals are exempt unless disclosing under FRAP 26.1(b). (Fed. Cir. R. 47.4)

docs.t: Fed. Cir. — Entry of appearance within 14 days, and one principal counsel
docs.x: Fed. Cir.. Entry of appearance within 14 days, and one principal counsel. Counsel retained before docketing file the form within 14 days after docketing, and designate one principal counsel. Counsel retained later file within 14 days of being retained or admitted, whichever is later. Counsel who don’t enter an appearance aren’t listed on the docket or any decision, intervenor and amicus counsel file with their first document, and a lawyer appearing for the first time after the case goes to a merits panel needs leave. Only counsel with an appearance on file may argue. Unrepresented parties file a notice of appearance within 14 days of docketing. (Fed. Cir. R. 47.3)

docs.t: Fed. Cir. — Confidential material: 15 unique words, 50 in two case types
docs.x: Fed. Cir.. Confidential material: 15 unique words, 50 in two case types. A motion, petition, response, reply, or brief may mark confidential up to 15 unique words, including numbers, and up to 50 in cases under 19 U.S.C. § 1516a or 28 U.S.C. § 1491(b). Marking is allowed only if the information is covered by a protective order and a statute, regulation, or rule authorizes it. Repeating the same material doesn’t use more of the allotment, and a response doesn’t count material the earlier filing already marked. The limit doesn’t apply to appendices, attachments, exhibits, and addenda. To mark more, move to waive. Redaction beyond FRAP 25(a)(5) and Rule 25.1 is prohibited, and counsel are solely responsible for what is redacted. (Fed. Cir. R. 25.1(d))

docs.t: Fed. Cir. — The appendix is filed after the reply brief
docs.x: Fed. Cir.. The appendix is filed after the reply brief. The appellant files the appendix within 7 days after the last reply brief is served and filed, or within the time for the reply if none is filed (and in a cross-appeal within 7 days after the time for the cross-appellant’s reply expires). The parties compile a designation of appendix material no later than 45 days before the appellant’s principal brief is due. Every appendix includes the entire docket sheet or certified list and, in a jury case, the charge, verdict, and interrogatory answers, and in a patent appeal the patents at issue in their entirety. Record parts not cited in the briefs stay out, and no volume may exceed 400 printed sheets, each with a table of contents and Roman-numeral volume cover. If the appellant fails to file it, the clerk may dismiss. (Fed. Cir. R. 30(a)(2); 30(b))

docs.t: Fed. Cir. — Six paper copies of each brief and the appendix
docs.x: Fed. Cir.. Six paper copies of each brief and the appendix. Six paper copies of each brief (three for an informal brief) and of any appendix go to the court on the schedule in Rule 25(c)(3), and when all parties have counsel, one more copy goes to principal counsel for the others unless they say it isn’t needed. No copies need go to amicus counsel. Page proofs may not be filed. (Fed. Cir. R. 31(b), 30(a)(3), 25(c)(3))

docs.t: Fed. Cir. — Electronic filing: before midnight Eastern
docs.x: Fed. Cir.. Electronic filing: before midnight Eastern. Unless the court sets a time, filing must be completed before midnight Eastern Time on the due date. Legal holidays include the day after Thanksgiving and any day the clerk’s office is closed by order. Timeliness of a response runs from service of the original, not any correction. (Fed. Cir. R. 26(a)(2))

docs.t: Fed. Cir. — The docketing statement is due in 14 days
docs.x: Fed. Cir.. The docketing statement is due in 14 days. Except for unrepresented parties, each appellant, cross-appellant, or petitioner files the clerk’s docketing statement within 14 days after docketing, which also satisfies FRAP 10(b)(3)(A)’s statement of issues. (Fed. Cir. R. 47.6)

docs.t: Fed. Cir. — Motions: say you consulted, and attach the certificate
docs.x: Fed. Cir.. Motions: say you consulted, and attach the certificate. Every motion has a caption, a statement of consent or opposition showing you discussed it with the other parties, a certificate of interest, and a declaration if the facts are disputed. A motion to expedite is labeled “Motion to Expedite” and proposes an expedited schedule. A motion to strike a brief is prohibited if you can respond in your own brief. Motions to dismiss, transfer, or remand should be made as soon as the grounds are known. (Fed. Cir. R. 27(a))

docs.t: Fed. Cir. — Patent claims go on the inside of the cover
docs.x: Fed. Cir.. Patent claims go on the inside of the cover. When the language of a patent or application is at issue, each party’s principal brief must reproduce illustrative claims inside the front cover, single-spaced if you like, and they don’t count toward the limit. “Nonconfidential” or “public” may appear on a cover only if there is a corresponding confidential version. (Fed. Cir. R. 32(a)(3))

docs.t: Fed. Cir. — Corrections need a Notice of Correction
docs.x: Fed. Cir.. Corrections need a Notice of Correction. You can’t fix a filed document with an errata sheet. File a corrected document marked “corrected” with a Notice of Correction listing each change, and file corrected paper copies if you’ve submitted them. Substantive changes need leave. (Fed. Cir. R. 25(i))

docs.t: Fed. Cir. — Oral argument: visual aids and conflicts
docs.x: Fed. Cir.. Oral argument: visual aids and conflicts. Tell the court by letter 14 days ahead if you’ll display a visual aid used at trial or an agency hearing, and 21 days ahead for any other, with notice to opposing counsel. Objections are due 7 days before argument. Presentation programs and projectors need leave on a motion filed 21 days before. When the clerk asks for scheduling conflicts you must answer within 7 days, with good cause shown for each conflict, even if you have none. (Fed. Cir. R. 34(c), (d))

docs.t: Fed. Cir. — No separate emergency-motion rule beyond FRAP
docs.x: Fed. Cir.. No separate emergency-motion rule beyond FRAP. Consi’s copy of the Federal Circuit Rules has no separate emergency-motion provision. For a stay or injunction pending appeal, follow FRAP 8 (move first in the district court or agency) and FRAP 27, and contact the Clerk’s Office before filing. (FRAP 8, 27; Fed. Cir. R. 27)

docs.t: SCOTUS — Cert petition due in 90 days
docs.x: SCOTUS. Cert petition due in 90 days. Ninety days from entry of judgment, or from the denial of rehearing if anyone timely sought it below. The clock doesn’t run from the mandate. The Clerk won’t file a petition that is jurisdictionally out of time. (Sup. Ct. R. 13.1, 13.3)

docs.x: SCOTUS. Extensions: one Justice, 60 days, apply 10 days early. A Justice may extend the time by up to 60 days for good cause. Merits briefs get 13,000 words, merits replies 6,000, and rehearing petitions 3,000. Attach a certificate stating your word count. (Sup. Ct. R. 33.1)

docs.t: D. Del. — Filing deadline: 5:00 p.m. Eastern
docs.x: D. Del.. Filing deadline: 5:00 p.m. Eastern. On the due date, filing must be completed by 5:00 p.m. Eastern, not midnight. Initial pleadings are the exception. Most federal courts use midnight, so this one catches people. (CM/ECF Administrative Procedures)

docs.x: D. Del.. 14 days to answer, 7 to reply. The answering brief is due 14 days after the opening brief, and the reply 7 days after the answering brief. The docket states the dates for you. (LR 7.1.2(b))

docs.x: D. Del.. Delaware counsel file everything. Once you’re in pro hac vice, Delaware counsel are the registered CM/ECF users and file all papers. (LR 83.5(d))

docs.x: D. Del.. No argument held back for the reply. The party filing the opening brief can’t reserve argument for the reply. (LR 7.1.3(a)(2))

docs.t: D. Del. — A nondispositive motion needs a phone call first
docs.x: D. Del.. A nondispositive motion needs a phone call first. Every nondispositive motion must come with an averment that counsel made a reasonable effort to reach agreement. A reasonable effort must include oral communication between Delaware counsel for both sides. A motion without the averment may be dismissed. Pro se cases and nonparty motions are exempt. (LR 7.1.1)

docs.t: D. Del. — The reply ends the briefing, apart from new authority
docs.x: D. Del.. The reply ends the briefing, apart from new authority. After the reply is served, no more papers are filed without court approval. The one exception is a non-argumentative cover letter that cites newly available authority and identifies the pending motion it affects. (LR 7.1.2(b), (c))

docs.t: D. Del. — Ask for oral argument within 7 days of the reply
docs.x: D. Del.. Ask for oral argument within 7 days of the reply. An application for oral argument must be in writing and made no later than 7 days after service of the reply brief. The court may grant it or deny it, or set argument on its own. (LR 7.1.4)

docs.t: D. Del. — Reargument: 14 days, 10 pages, rarely granted
docs.x: D. Del.. Reargument: 14 days, 10 pages, rarely granted. A motion for reargument is due within 14 days after the court’s decision. Rule 59(e) motions follow Rule 59(e)’s own deadline. The motion and the answer, due 14 days after filing, are each limited to 10 pages, and no reply is allowed unless the court grants one. You can’t move for reargument of a magistrate judge’s ruling. Object under Rule 72 and LR 72.1(b) instead. (LR 7.1.5)

docs.t: D. Del. — A motion to amend needs a redline
docs.x: D. Del.. A motion to amend needs a redline. Attach the signed proposed pleading with its exhibits, plus a second version marked to show the changes, with deleted text in brackets or struck through and added text underlined. (LR 15.1(a))

docs.t: D. Del. — A discovery motion must quote the discovery
docs.x: D. Del.. A discovery motion must quote the discovery. Put a verbatim recitation of each interrogatory, request, answer, response, or objection in the motion or the brief, or attach a copy of the discovery document. (LR 37.1)

docs.t: D. Del. — Don’t file discovery. File a notice of service
docs.x: D. Del.. Don’t file discovery. File a notice of service. When every party has counsel, discovery requests, responses, and Rule 26(a) disclosures are served but not filed. File a Notice of Service certifying what was served, when, and how. A deposition notice or proof of service of a subpoena counts as the notice. (LR 5.4(b))

docs.t: D. Del. — Ask to extend a deadline before it passes
docs.x: D. Del.. Ask to extend a deadline before it passes. A request to extend discovery deadlines or postpone trial must be made by motion or stipulation before the deadline expires, and it must state the reasons. (LR 16.4)

docs.t: D. Del. — Bill of costs: meet and confer, then 28 days
docs.x: D. Del.. Bill of costs: meet and confer, then 28 days. The prevailing party files a bill of costs within 28 days after the appeal time expires or the mandate issues, after meeting and conferring about what is taxable. Missing the deadline or skipping the procedure waives costs unless the court orders otherwise. (LR 54.1(a))

An early summary judgment motion (even a partial one) decided on the merits bars a second one after discovery unless the court has expressly allowed it. Cite docketed documents as “Doc. The judge ordinarily holds hearings on motions to dismiss (especially complicated ones or where dismissing the whole case is under consideration) and on summary judgment motions, with no set time limits.

docs.x: Judge Leo T. Sorokin, D. Mass.. Courtesy copies (trap): Deliver one paper courtesy copy to the District Court Clerk’s Office of any motion memorandum and its accompanying papers when those papers (excluding the memorandum) exceed 100 pages (the 2025 general-practices order describes it as the memorandum plus exhibits exceeding 100 pages). docs.t: Judge Leo T. Sorokin (D. Mass.) — Discovery and protective orders
docs.x: Judge Leo T. Sorokin, D. Mass.. Discovery and protective orders: No requirements beyond L.R. 37.1, but the judge encourages requesting a status conference or filing a joint status report instead of a motion, in a repeating format: the request and response, the complaining party’s explanation of why more is needed, and the other party’s explanation of why the response is adequate. The judge often decides discovery motions but sometimes refers them, or whole cases, to a magistrate judge. Emergency discovery motions are discouraged and considered only in extraordinary circumstances. In complex cases a default protective order applies until the court adopts a stipulated order: material designated “Confidential Pursuant to the Court’s Default PO” may be seen only by outside counsel and the court.

docs.t: Judge Leo T. Sorokin (D. Mass.) — Scheduling and remote appearances
docs.x: Judge Leo T. Sorokin, D. Mass.. Scheduling and remote appearances: Submit a joint statement under L.R. 16.1. The schedule typically sets a dispositive-motion deadline after all discovery, about 12 months after the Rule 16 conference, with a status conference after fact discovery. Daubert deadlines are set at the initial pretrial conference. Rule 16 and status conferences are typically held by Zoom. Other proceedings are in person, though the judge will consider a Zoom non-evidentiary motion hearing or pretrial conference on request for a good reason.

docs.x: Judge Leo T. Sorokin, D. Mass.. Pretrial (civil): Deadlines come in an order setting the case for trial, issued after the initial pretrial conference. Rule 26(a)(3) disclosures and written objections are exchanged by set dates; undisclosed objections (other than under FRE 402 and 403) are waived. The parties must meet in person before the final pretrial conference and file a joint pretrial memorandum under L.R. 16.5(D), including a “List of Uncontested Exhibits” numbered in one sequence regardless of proponent and a list of objected-to exhibits lettered in one sequence of capital letters. docs.t: Judge Leo T. Sorokin (D. Mass.) — Trial
docs.x: Judge Leo T. Sorokin, D. Mass.. Trial: Trial runs 9 a.m. to 1 p.m. with one mid-morning break, day to day; deliberating juries sit full days. Bench trials may run full days or afternoons. Bring two paper copies of exhibits in binders (one for the judge, one for the law clerk) at the start of trial, and pre-mark exhibits. Counsel use the podium. Disclose chalks to opposing counsel early enough for objections without delay. The judge conducts voir dire, with sidebar follow-up; peremptories are exercised on jurors seated in the box, then only on replacements. Civil juries are 12; criminal alternates are usually 2 (up to 6). The judge circulates a draft charge before the charge conference and gives the jury a written copy.

docs.t: Judge Leo T. Sorokin (D. Mass.) — Criminal and sentencing
docs.x: Judge Leo T. Sorokin, D. Mass.. Criminal and sentencing: The judge enforces the suppression-motion deadline set by the magistrate judge unless circumstances justify a change, and usually holds hearings on review of detention orders. Sentencing memoranda are encouraged in every case, and the parties are encouraged to address restorative justice principles. Where there are identifiable victims, the judge offers a pre-sentencing status conference with them on the record.

docs.t: Judge Angel Kelley (D. Mass.) — Dispositive motion briefing (trap)
docs.x: Judge Angel Kelley, D. Mass.. Dispositive motion briefing (trap): “Dispositive motions” here include motions to dismiss, for summary judgment, for judgment on the pleadings, and for judgment as a matter of law. Oppositions are due within 14 days of service (21 days for summary judgment). The movant may reply as of right within 7 days of the opposition (summary judgment: within 14 days after the opposition is served), limited to 10 pages. Sur-replies are not permitted. Memoranda are limited to 20 pages under L.R. 7.1(b)(4); longer papers need leave. Request oral argument in a separate paragraph of the motion or opposition; otherwise the motion is decided on the papers.

docs.t: Judge Angel Kelley (D. Mass.) — Summary judgment (trap)
docs.x: Judge Angel Kelley, D. Mass.. Summary judgment (trap): The movant states its facts in a numbered list. The opponent repeats each fact verbatim in the same order with “RESPONSE: [Not disputed/Disputed]” and record citations immediately beneath, then lists additional facts in the same document numbered consecutively after the movant’s. The movant’s reply follows the same process. Cross-motions: defendant moves first (20-page memorandum) by the scheduling-order date; within 30 days plaintiff files one combined opposition and cross-motion (30 pages); within 21 days defendant files one combined reply and opposition (15 pages); within 14 days plaintiff may reply (5 pages).

docs.t: Judge Angel Kelley (D. Mass.) — Exhibits and citations
docs.x: Judge Angel Kelley, D. Mass.. Exhibits and citations: File exhibits in the order they first appear in the motion and memorandum, labeled by number (Exhibit 1), not by letter. Cite docketed documents as “(Doc No. ___)” so ECF Citation Links work, not by title or Bluebook format. If restricted personal data (full SSNs or account numbers, minors’ names, full birth dates, home addresses) is mentioned in court, any right to have it stricken or redacted is waived.

Copies must be double-sided, include exhibit tabs, be marked “COURTESY COPY – DO NOT SCAN,” and be delivered within 5 business days of e-filing. Litigants proceeding in forma pauperis are exempt.

docs.x: Judge Angel Kelley, D. Mass.. Discovery motions (trap): Motions to compel, for protective orders, to quash, and to strike discovery responses must be filed by the close of fact or expert discovery, whichever applies, absent good cause. The supporting memorandum must quote each disputed interrogatory, deposition question, request, or other item and its response, with the movant’s position and legal authority immediately after each item. The judge often decides discovery motions but may refer them to the magistrate judge, and decides case by case whether to hold a hearing. File any proposed protective order as early as possible.

docs.x: Judge Angel Kelley, D. Mass.. Scheduling and remote appearances: File the L.R. 16.1 joint statement with a proposed schedule following the Sample Scheduling Order no later than 7 days before the scheduling conference, and state whether the parties consent to trial by a magistrate judge. The court may adopt the joint proposal without a conference. In pro se cases, separate proposals are accepted if the parties cannot agree. Where one defendant has answered and another has moved to dismiss, the court may hold a Rule 16 conference so discovery can begin among the non-moving parties. All conferences and hearings are in person in Courtroom 8. Only scheduling and status conferences may be moved to Zoom, on a joint request (by email to the courtroom clerk) at least 2 business days before.

docs.x: Judge Margaret R. Guzman, D. Mass.. Other motions and replies (trap): The form scheduling order allows a reply on any motion without leave if it is no more than 12 pages, double-spaced, and filed within 7 days (excluding intermediate weekends and holidays) after service of the opposition; otherwise replies and surreplies need leave, and the proposed brief may be attached to the motion for leave. Motions to compel, for protective orders, to quash, and similar motions must be filed by the close of fact or expert discovery, whichever applies, and in time for a ruling before the deadline. docs.t: Judge Margaret R. Guzman (D. Mass.) — Sentencing (trap)
docs.x: Judge Margaret R. Guzman, D. Mass.. Sentencing (trap): Any sentencing memorandum is due 7 days before sentencing, with a copy to Probation; a party not filing one must notify the Clerk (by email or docket entry) at least 7 days before. Guideline and non-guideline arguments go in a single filing. At least 5 days before sentencing, advise the court of legal questions the PSR does not adequately address and any factual issues needing an evidentiary hearing. PSR objections are due 14 days after disclosure. For sentencing within 4 weeks of the Rule 11 hearing, the defendant must knowingly waive the interview or PSR objections. The government should give notice of any victim impact statement and how it will be made (preferably from the stand, not under oath). In revocations, give notice of any stipulation to violations or request for imprisonment.

docs.t: Judge Margaret R. Guzman (D. Mass.) — Default judgment (trap)
docs.x: Judge Margaret R. Guzman, D. Mass.. Default judgment (trap): Move for default judgment within 30 days of the entry of default, or show good cause; otherwise the claims may be dismissed for want of prosecution. Support the motion with affidavits on the sum certain (Rule 55(b)(1) only), the defaulting party’s non-infant, competent, non-military status, damages, and costs, completed no later than 14 days after filing; under Rule 55(b)(1) also file the posted proposed judgment form. Noncompliant motions may be denied and interest, costs, or fees refused.

docs.x: Judge Allison D. Burroughs, D. Mass.. Sealed filings and courtesy copies (trap): Sealed documents may not be filed electronically. Once a motion to seal is granted, upload the sealed documents to the secure dropbox link the docket clerk provides; if the motion to seal itself must be sealed, email the docket clerk for a link. For numerous sealed documents or media files that cannot be e-filed, give the court a USB/flash drive with the main document, memorandum, and exhibits as separate, clearly named PDFs, not password-protected, each no larger than 50mb. Do not submit paper courtesy copies of any electronic filing unless the court asks for them. The judge’s survey answers also direct counsel to “file unredacted copies as exhibits to redacted” filings.

docs.t: Judge Allison D. Burroughs (D. Mass.) — Motions and briefing
docs.x: Judge Allison D. Burroughs, D. Mass.. Motions and briefing: Replies and surreplies are allowed when requested and reasonable, limited to 10 pages absent leave; keep them brief. Motions to dismiss and for summary judgment are heard only if the judge thinks argument would help. Post-argument briefs only on request when helpful. On summary judgment the judge encourages a joint statement of disputed (or undisputed) facts, as in state court practice, so each side’s view of each fact appears in one document. No courtesy copies of dispositive-motion materials are required.

docs.t: Judge Allison D. Burroughs (D. Mass.) — Discovery (trap)
docs.x: Judge Allison D. Burroughs, D. Mass.. Discovery (trap): In some cases the judge asks parties to start with letters rather than motions; if an issue cannot be addressed in a letter of 2 pages or less, file a motion. The judge typically decides discovery motions, without a hearing, and quickly; frequent filers may be referred to a magistrate judge. Emergency discovery motions are considered unless the parties abuse them. Ask for fact-discovery extensions before the deadline passes. Bifurcated discovery is disfavored except for largely unrelated, non-overlapping topics.

docs.x: Judge Allison D. Burroughs, D. Mass.. Protective orders (trap): Any proposed protective order must include this language: “The Court may allow, after notice to the parties, the disclosure of any document or information covered by this Protective Order, and may modify this Protective Order at any time in the interests of justice, and to ensure that any proceeding before this Court is fair, efficient, and consistent with the public interest.”

docs.t: Judge Allison D. Burroughs (D. Mass.) — Scheduling and remote appearances
docs.x: Judge Allison D. Burroughs, D. Mass.. Scheduling and remote appearances: In routine cases, propose a schedule that makes the case trial-ready within 1 year of the initial scheduling conference. The judge sets a schedule through fact discovery (and summary judgment or expert discovery if clearly needed) and holds a status conference at the end of fact discovery. The judge often sets the schedule on the parties’ written proposal; say whether you object to that. A call or conference is set if there is no joint proposal or the proposed schedule seems long. Rule 16 conferences need not be in person. In criminal cases the initial status conference after the case returns from the magistrate judge may be by telephone; Zoom may be used for setting trial dates in large civil cases.

docs.t: Judge Allison D. Burroughs (D. Mass.) — Pretrial
docs.x: Judge Allison D. Burroughs, D. Mass.. Pretrial: Trial briefs are required in civil cases and preferred in criminal cases. Proposed voir dire, jury instructions, verdict forms, witness and exhibit lists, and motions in limine should be filed at least 2 weeks before trial; the judge may ask for jury instructions by email to the courtroom deputy. No page limit for motions in limine; they are heard at the final pretrial conference. Daubert motions are resolved earlier in the case.
